name: Shelf Zipline Network
description: An improvised network of cables strung between Shelf buildings, used with simple pulley harnesses for rapid transit between rooftops and upper floors. The Zipline Network grew organically over decades — whenever someone needed to get from Building A to Building B without going down to street level, they strung a cable. Now the network covers most of The Shelf's residential blocks, and experienced users can traverse the entire district without touching the ground. The cables are maintained by the community with varying degrees of competence. Testing a line before you ride it is not paranoia — it's survival.
speed: 20-40 km/h depending on angle and rider weight
autonomy: Manual only. Grip strength is your safety system.
common_usage: Rooftop-to-rooftop transit, avoiding street-level hazards, courier shortcuts, children's play (terrifyingly).
story_hooks: The Zipline Network forms the backbone of a communications system — messages are passed at connection points, creating a telegraph that no electronics can detect
Someone is cutting ziplines at night, isolating specific buildings from the network and from help
related_entities: Ringo Corponation SlipThread MX-3 Urban Cable Micro-Mobility Rig
physical_description: Weathered steel cables, some corroded to a dull rust-brown patina, crisscross between blocky concrete and prefab structures at varying heights and angles. Pulley harnesses are jury-rigged affairs—repurposed climbing gear, salvaged industrial pulleys, frayed rope, and zip-tie reinforcements, each one slightly different from the next. The cables sag noticeably in places, some wrapped in faded electrical tape or cloth to improve grip; spray-painted warning marks and community symbols mark known trouble spots.
